title: Muslim electorate in Karnataka shrinks 18.84 per cent after SIR, slightly above State average
shows: Frontline reports estimates by Sankalp, a political research consultancy in Karnataka, of how the fall in Karnataka's roll divides by religion. The roll does not record religion, and the magazine says Sankalp's figures by religion are estimates. Karnataka's roll fell from 5.54 crore electors before the revision to 4.55 crore on the final roll, or 17.9 per cent. By Sankalp's estimate Muslim electors fell from 71.56 lakh to 58.08 lakh, or 18.84 per cent, and other electors from 4.82 crore to 3.96 crore, or 17.79 per cent, so the Muslim share of the roll went from 12.91 per cent to 12.77 per cent. In Bengaluru's 28 seats the roll fell from 1.03 crore to 59.08 lakh, and Sankalp puts the fall at 33.72 per cent for Muslim electors and 43.82 per cent for others. In the other 196 seats it puts the fall at 15.32 per cent for Muslim electors and 12.18 per cent for others. The political analyst Sandeep Shastri tells the magazine that Bengaluru's roll had long been inflated by electors living abroad or voting in their home towns. Of the 1,07,96,339 names left off the draft, Sankalp counted 15.43 lakh as Muslim names and 92.32 lakh as others. It also counts 39 of the 224 seats where booths that gave 60 per cent or more of their votes in the 2024 Lok Sabha election to the Congress hold more than 35 per cent of the seat's names left off the draft. Across those 39 seats 42 per cent of the names left off are in such booths, and 26 of the seats are held by the Congress, 11 by the BJP and 2 by the Janata Dal (Secular). Frontline reports, from sources in the office of Karnataka's Chief Electoral Officer, that 716 foreign nationals were found on the roll, 641 of them from Nepal.
quote: Electoral rolls do not record an elector’s religion, so Sankalp’s religion-wise figures are estimates.
While the number of Muslim electors reduced from 71.56 lakh to 58.08 lakh, the number of non-Muslim voters reduced from 4.82 crore to 3.96 crore.

title: ECI’s belated U-turn doesn’t undo the injustice of mass exclusions
authors: Anjali Bhardwaj, Amrita Johri, Yogendra Yadav
shows: Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri, RTI activists with the Satark Nagrik Sangathan and the NCPRI who are petitioners on the Delhi SIR in the Supreme Court, and Yogendra Yadav of Swaraj India and the Bharat Jodo Abhiyan, read the Commission's letter of 6 November to the Chief Electoral Officers of Delhi, Maharashtra, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland. By their account it waives the deadline for enumeration forms in those seven states and lets an elector who has moved come back to the roll on the enumeration form with a new address in place of Form 6. It lets a homeless elector be added on a field check by the booth level officer. It invokes Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, under which a registration officer can correct a name left out by inadvertence or error, and it gives a restored elector the old EPIC number. They give 4.52 crore names left off the draft in the seven states and 13.3 crore across India. They tie the letter to the Supreme Court's hearing of 28 October, when the bench called the use of Form 6 for such electors an error and a structural incongruity, and they set it beside the Commission's clarification of 3 November that a Form 6 filed by such an elector would not be treated as a false declaration. They ask why the same relief is not open in Bengaluru or in states such as Bihar and West Bengal where the revision is over, and whether electors who have already filed Form 6 will get their old numbers back. They argue that the revision still places on the elector the burden of being on the roll and that it should be withdrawn.
quote: It offers multiple reliefs to the 4.52 crore voters whose names were excluded from the draft SIR electoral rolls in these states.
In another welcome turnaround, the ECI now directs that those excluded voters whose names are restored will be reassigned their old EPIC number.

title: ECI and its black box: How the election body denies the right to know
shows: Venkatesh Nayak, director of the Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative, writes that he asked the Commission under the RTI Act in May 2026 for the reports of the Chief Electoral Rolls Observers it sent to 12 states and union territories in the second phase of the SIR, West Bengal among them. He says the Commission refused, citing a decision of the Central Information Commission of 2010. He says it refused his earlier request for the reports of its Expenditure Observers from the 2024 Lok Sabha election on the same ground and sent him its internal circulars of 2016 and 2022, which list observers' reports among the information to be refused under the Act. He argues that most exemptions in the Act carry a test of harm, that the 2010 decision accepted the Commission's claims of a fiduciary relationship with its observers and of danger to them without question and made no mention of S P Gupta v. President of India (1981), and that information commissioners since have not weighed the public interest as the Act requires. He opens with the claim of the former Special Roll Observer for West Bengal that the observer had no prior knowledge of the Chief Electoral Officer's appeals against electors the judicial officers had cleared, and with the Commission's statement to the Court that it had only a communication after the appeals were filed.
quote: In May this year, I sought under RTI copies of reports of the ECI’s Chief Electoral Rolls Observers deputed during SIR-II to 12 states and Union Territories, including West Bengal.
The ECI denied access, citing a 16-year-old decision by the Central Information Commission (CIC).

title: Epic failures: on electoral roll, welfare
shows: The Hindu's editorial takes up the statement of Rajiv Ranjan Singh, the Union Minister of Panchayati Raj, that voter identity cards with biometric authentication will replace Aadhaar in identifying beneficiaries and making payments under his Ministry's schemes, and says it runs contrary to existing laws and regulations. It recalls the Supreme Court's judgment of 27 May on the Bihar SIR, which allowed the Commission only a limited enquiry into citizenship whose consequences are confined to the roll and the vote, and which called the EPIC a derivative document issued on the basis of inclusion in the roll. It also recalls the Court's observations on petitions against West Bengal's orders removing people deleted from the roll from the Public Distribution System and the Annapurna Yojana. It says 93% of the appeals heard in West Bengal for reinstatement had ended with names restored by September 2026, and that the Court has yet to decide whether the Commission's method of logical discrepancies is lawful. It argues that the BJP-led coalition sees the smaller rolls as a way to limit welfare, and asks the Court to decide the petitions against the SIR and to say again that its rolls cannot be used to curtail welfare.
quote: Not every citizen is an eligible voter, and tying benefits to the electoral roll is illogical and also cruel.
In the appeals heard for reinstatement, 93% resulted in the restoration of names by September 2026, pointing to massive pre-election disenfranchisement.
